newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK blasts China for leaking PLA recce party details.
newsitem.headline: HK blasts China for leaking PLA recce party details.

text.p: The Hong Kong government on Monday strongly criticised a senior Chinese official for leaking confidential information on mainland Chinese troops to be stationed in the territory ahead of the handover next year.

The government charged that the leaked details had come from confidential discussions of the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG), which handles matters relating to Hong Kong's transfer to Chinese rule.
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China at midnight on June 30, 1997 when the People's Liberation Army (PLA) will replace the British military garrison.

"We were shocked therefore to see details of these talks being publicly revealed by a senior Chinese official," the government said in a statement. "This is a serious breach of JLG confidentiality about which we have protested strongly to the Chinese side."

Cheng Shousan, deputy director of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, told a Hong Kong television station on Sunday that China was looking to send an advance party of PLA troops to Hong Kong ahead of the handover.
Cheng was quoted as saying the 300-member party would include soldiers and medical and communications staff, and would be housed in closed barracks.
But the Hong Kong government said China's request to station a PLA advance party in the territory was still being discussed.

"We must emphasise again that no decision has been taken and no agreement has been reached on the Chinese side's request for the stationing of PLA advance personnel in Hong Kong before the handover," the statement said.

The arrival of the PLA is viewed with some trepidation in Hong Kong where the images of its troops cracking down on the student-led pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989 remains etched in the colony's collective memory.

"The community is naturally very sensitive about this issue and would expect the British side to proceed carefully and cautiously," the statement said. "The Governor (Chris Patten) has made it clear that any arrangement agreed would involve a minimum number of troops, who would be subject to Hong Kong law before July 1, 1997."

It also said it did not see the need for members of the advance party to bring weapons with them. "We do not see the need for this, nor do we believe the community would see that this was either necessary or desirable," the statement said.
